young.html: Socrates lived in Athens about 2,400 years ago. He did not write books. He walked around the city asking people questions: What is courage? What is fairness? What makes a person good? Most people thought they knew the answers, until Socrates asked a few more questions.

A friend once asked the priestess of the god Apollo at Delphi whether anyone was wiser than Socrates. The answer came back: no one. Socrates was puzzled, because he did not think he was wise. So he went to people who were famous for being wise and questioned them. He found that they did not really know what they claimed to know. He decided that his only wisdom was this: he knew that he did not know.

Some powerful people grew tired of his questions. When Socrates was about 70, three men took him to court. A jury of about 500 citizens found him guilty, and he was sentenced to death. His friends offered to help him escape from prison, but he said no: he had lived under the laws of Athens all his life, and he would not break them now.
His student Plato wrote down the story in four short books: Euthyphro, the Apology (which means a speech of defense, not saying sorry), Crito and Phaedo.

young.html: Play Socrates. Pick a word everyone uses, like fair or brave. Ask someone in your family what it means. Then think of an example that doesn't fit their answer (“Is it brave to run into traffic for a ball?”). Help them improve the answer. Take turns. You are doing what Socrates did: testing an idea with questions.

full.html: Socrates (c. 470–399 BC) spent his life in Athens, served as a soldier in the Peloponnesian War, and became famous for questioning people in public. He wrote nothing. We know him through his students, above all Plato (c. 428–348 BC), through the soldier and writer Xenophon, and through a comedy, Aristophanes' Clouds (423 BC), which made fun of him.

In 399 BC, a few years after Athens lost the war with Sparta, three citizens, Meletus, Anytus and Lycon, charged Socrates with impiety (not honoring the city's gods and bringing in new ones) and with corrupting the young. Many historians think politics played a part: some of Socrates' companions had been tied to the harsh rulers who governed Athens just after the war. The charges themselves were religious ones.
Plato tells the story in four dialogues. They are short, and they are the best place to start reading Plato.

On his way to court, Socrates meets Euthyphro, an expert in religious matters who is taking his own father to court over a worker's death, and is sure that this is the holy thing to do. Socrates asks him what holiness is. Euthyphro gives an example, then a definition (“what the gods love”), then a better one (“what all the gods love”). Socrates then asks the famous question:

full.text: The point which I should first wish to understand is whether the pious or holy is beloved by the gods because it is holy, or holy because it is beloved of the gods.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.html: This is the Euthyphro question. If the gods love something because it is holy, then holiness is something in its own right, and “loved by the gods” only describes it. If something is holy only because the gods love it, holiness seems to depend on their choice. Euthyphro picks the first, which means his definition did not say what holiness is. Philosophers and religious thinkers have discussed the question ever since, and have given many different answers.
“Apology” comes from the Greek apologia, a speech of defense. Socrates tells the jury he is no clever speaker, then explains how his habit of questioning began, with the oracle at Delphi.

full.text: …the truth is, O men of Athens, that God only is wise; and by his answer he intends to show that the wisdom of men is worth little or nothing; he is not speaking of Socrates, he is only using my name by way of illustration, as if he said, He, O men, is the wisest, who, like Socrates, knows that his wisdom is in truth worth nothing.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.html: He cross-examines his accuser Meletus in front of the jury, catching him in contradictions. He says he is like a gadfly sent to keep a large, sleepy horse awake: the city needs someone to sting it into thinking. He says he has always followed an inner voice, his daimonion, which warns him when he is about to do something wrong.

The jury votes him guilty. By the usual reckoning the vote was about 280 to 220, and Socrates remarks that thirty votes the other way would have freed him. In Athens the accused then proposed a penalty. Socrates first says that he deserves free meals at public expense, like an Olympic champion, and then offers a fine his friends will pay. The jury votes for death. Here is part of his reason for not simply going quietly into exile:

full.text: …if I say again that daily to discourse about virtue, and of those other things about which you hear me examining myself and others, is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living, you are still less likely to believe me.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.cap: Move the slider on the trial scene to see how many votes had to change. In Athens a tie set the accused free.

full.title: Thirty votes
full.q: Suppose a jury of 500 voted 280 guilty and 220 not guilty, and a tie means acquittal. How many jurors would have had to change their vote?
steps: Each switched vote takes one from 280 and adds one to 220, so the gap of 60 closes by 2 each time.
After 30 switches the vote is 250 to 250, a tie.
A tie acquits, so 30 votes would have been enough.

full.html: Socrates waits about a month in prison, because no executions could happen until a sacred ship returned from the island of Delos. His old friend Crito comes before dawn: the guards are paid, and friends will hide him in Thessaly. Socrates says they must reason it out, as always. They agree on a starting point:

full.text: Soc. …I should like to know whether I may say the same of another proposition—that not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued? Cr. Yes, that also remains unshaken. Soc. And a good life is equivalent to a just and honourable one—that holds also? Cr. Yes, it does.
full.author: Plato
full.ed: The Dialogues of Plato, 3rd edition, vol. II, Clarendon Press

full.html: Socrates then imagines the Laws of Athens speaking to him. They raised and educated him; for seventy years he was free to leave and chose to stay; that is a kind of agreement. If he runs now, he does wrong in return for wrong, which he holds is never right. He stays.

The argument in the Crito is one of the first statements of the idea that living in a society can be a kind of agreement with its laws. Later writers, from Locke to Rousseau on this ladder, built theories of a social contract. Others have read the same dialogue as a case for following one's conscience, because in the Apology Socrates also says he would not stop questioning even if the court ordered him to. Readers still argue about how the two fit together.
Thinking “apology” means Socrates said sorry. He did the opposite: he defended his whole way of life and refused to beg.
The last day, spent talking about whether the soul outlives the body, is the next rung on this ladder. It ends with Socrates drinking the poison, calmly, among his friends.

Plato or Socrates? Plato was in the courtroom (he says so in the Apology) but these are his works, written years later. Scholars think the Apology is fairly close to what Socrates said, but nobody can be sure how much is Plato's own.

deep.html: Three sources disagree. Aristophanes' Clouds shows a fussy teacher who studies the sky and teaches tricks of argument for money, which Socrates denies in the Apology. Xenophon's Memorabilia and his own short Apology show a practical, pious man giving sound advice. Plato's Socrates is ironic, probing and always asking “what is it?” Historians call the puzzle of the real Socrates the Socratic problem.

Socrates' way of questioning has a Greek name, elenchus, “testing” or “refutation”. Someone offers a definition; Socrates gets agreement on some other points; then he shows that those points contradict the definition. The person ends up puzzled. Socrates thought puzzlement was progress, because you cannot look for an answer you think you already have. Teachers and lawyers still use a version of this method.

items: Is it ever right to break a law? What would Socrates in the Crito say, and what would Socrates in the Apology say?
Does knowing that you don't know make you wiser than someone who is sure?
If a jury is fair but makes a wrong decision, should you still accept it?

deep.html: Later books answer back. Aristotle (on this ladder) named the Socratic “what is it?” question as the start of the search for definitions. The Stoics, such as Epictetus, made Socrates their model of calm in the face of death. Martin Luther King Jr.'s “Letter from Birmingham Jail” (1963) points to Socrates when it explains breaking an unjust law openly and accepting the penalty.

questions: Socrates said he was wise only because he knew he didn't know. Can you think of a time when admitting you didn't know something helped you?
Was Socrates right to stay in prison when his friends could have helped him escape? What would you have told him?
Socrates said “the unexamined life is not worth living.” What do you think it means to examine your life?
Is something good because people like it, or do people like it because it is good? Try it with a game, a food and an act of kindness.
Socrates called himself a gadfly that keeps a city awake. Is it helpful or annoying to have someone around who questions everything? Both?
Why do you think Plato wrote these books as conversations instead of essays?
care: These dialogues end with Socrates' death by a cup of poison, which Plato describes calmly and without anything graphic. Young readers can start with the Apology and the Crito.
